titleText.es: ¡Ese sombrero es mío! ¡Me has quitado el sombrero!
titleText.en: That's my hat! You took my hat!
titleText.noteEn: The title text calls attention to the hat taken during the silent final panels.

regions.labelEs: ME DOY CUENTA DE LO QUE HAS HECHO.

applications.explanationEn: Me matches the speaker, doy is the corresponding form of dar, cuenta completes the fixed expression, and de introduces what has become clear.
Lo que refers to an already understood action or situation without naming it as a specific masculine or feminine noun.
Has is the helper for one familiar person, and hecho is hacer's completed-action form.

regions.labelEs: TRATABAS DE QUE ME ABRIERA A TI PARA PODER HERIR MIS SENTIMIENTOS.

applications.explanationEn: The -abas ending presents the past attempt as ongoing background rather than as one bounded, completed event.
Tratabas de que introduces an attempted action by a different person, and me abriera puts that intended action in the matching special past form.
Me and abriera describe the speaker opening up, while a ti identifies the person receiving that openness.
Para introduces a purpose, and poder remains in its unchanged dictionary form ending in -er.
Poder expresses ability, and the following action herir stays in its unchanged dictionary form.

regions.labelEs: TE GUSTA HACER DAÑO A LA GENTE.

applications.explanationEn: Te identifies the person experiencing the liking, gusta presents the activity as pleasing, and hacer stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Hacer daño forms the harm expression, and a la gente supplies the affected group.

regions.labelEs: PUES A MÍ TAMBIÉN ME GUSTA HACER DAÑO.

applications.explanationEn: Me identifies the speaker as the person experiencing the liking, gusta presents the activity as pleasing, and hacer stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Hacer and daño form the fixed harm collocation here without an explicitly named target.
Lo stands for the already understood action and appears directly before the changed verb hago.
Mejor supplies the irregular comparative “better,” and que opens the other side of the comparison.

regions.labelEs: VOY A HACERTE MÁS DAÑO DEL QUE TÚ PODRÍAS HACERME NUNCA A MÍ.

applications.explanationEn: Voy matches the speaker, a links to the action, and hacer remains in its unchanged dictionary form inside hacerte.
Te is attached to the end of the unchanged verb hacer and marks one familiar person as affected.
Hacerte carries the affected person inside the verb, daño completes the harm collocation, and más only increases its amount.
Más sets a greater amount of the masculine noun daño, so the following comparison uses del que before its second action.
Podrías supplies the conditional form of poder, while hacer stays in its unchanged dictionary form inside hacerme.
Me is attached to the unchanged verb hacer and marks the speaker as the affected person.
He is the speaker's present helper, and penetrado is penetrar's completed-action form.

regions.labelEs: DE TODA LA GENTE QUE CONOCERÁS, SÓLO YO TE ENTIENDO.

applications.explanationEn: Conocerás keeps the whole verb conocer and adds -ás for what one familiar person will do.

regions.labelEs: Y NO ME VERÁS NUNCA MÁS.

applications.explanationEn: Verás keeps the whole verb ver and adds -ás for what one familiar person will do.
Nunca supplies the negative and más extends it into “again” or “anymore.”
No stays before the verb because nunca más follows it; Spanish keeps both negative elements together for one negative meaning.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks an “I” verb that is used with me
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs conventionally come with me, te, se, nos, or os even when no one literally acts on themselves. Me marks the speaker's form. English usually absorbs it into the verb's meaning.

example.en: I complain about the noise.

cards.promptEs: darse cuenta de (que) + hecho o situación
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone realizes or becomes aware of something?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching small pronoun, a form of dar, cuenta, and then de before what is realized.
cards.noteEn: The small pronoun and dar must match the person: me doy cuenta, te das cuenta, se da cuenta, nos damos cuenta, and so on. Use de before a noun and de que before a full statement. Cuenta is not translated separately in this expression.

example.es: Nos dimos cuenta de que faltaba una llave.
example.en: We realized that a key was missing.

cards.answerEn: I realize (as part of me doy cuenta)
cards.noteEn: Doy normally means “I give.” In the expression darse cuenta, the matching form of dar combines with cuenta to mean “to realize” or “to notice.”

example.en: I realize the mistake.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes darse cuenta, “to realize”
cards.noteEn: Cuenta can mean an account, bill, or calculation. In darse cuenta, it is part of a fixed expression and is not translated separately.

example.es: Ella se dio cuenta muy tarde.
example.en: She realized very late.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; introduces what is realized after darse cuenta
cards.noteEn: After darse cuenta, de introduces the fact or thing that becomes clear. Before a full statement, Spanish normally uses de que.

example.es: Se dio cuenta de que era tarde.
example.en: She realized that it was late.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Lo combines with que to refer to an idea, action, or whole situation rather than a masculine noun. Together, lo que means “what” or “the thing that.”

example.en: I understand what you’re saying.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “what” or “the thing that” without naming a specific object?
cards.answerEn: Use lo que to refer to an idea, action, situation, or unnamed thing.
cards.noteEn: Here lo is neutral: it does not stand for a masculine noun. Que introduces the information that identifies the idea or thing. Together they work as one unit.

example.en: I don't understand what you're saying.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Here que completes lo que, a neutral expression meaning “what” or “the thing that.” It does not refer to a particular masculine or feminine noun.

example.en: I understand what you’re saying.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

example.en: I have finished.

cards.noteEn: Hecho is the irregular completed-action form of hacer, “to do” or “to make.” After a form of haber, it corresponds to English “done.”

example.en: I have already done the homework.

cards.noteEn: Tratabas is a past form of tratar for one familiar person. With de before an action, tratar means “to try”; the -abas ending presents that attempt as ongoing or as background rather than as one completed event.

example.en: You were trying to open the door.

cards.answerEn: Use the preterite for a completed event and the imperfect for background, an ongoing situation, or something that used to happen.
cards.noteEn: Think of a story: the preterite answers “What happened next?” The imperfect answers “What was happening?”, “What were things like?”, or “What used to happen?” These two names describe how the speaker presents an event, not simply how long it lasted.
cards.questionEn: Spanish has two common ways to talk about the past. When do you use each one?

example.en: While I was walking, it started to rain.

cards.promptEs: tratar de que + otra persona + subjuntivo
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone tries to get a different person to do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of tratar, then de que, then identify the other person and put that person's action in a special subjunctive form.
cards.noteEn: For the same person's action, use tratar de plus the verb's unchanged dictionary form: trato de salir (“I try to leave”). When the intended action belongs to someone else, use de que and the subjunctive, a special form for an intended action not stated as fact: trato de que Marta salga. After a past form of tratar, that action often uses a past subjunctive form such as saliera.

example.es: Tratamos de que Ana llegue temprano.
example.en: We try to get Ana to arrive early.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; a required verb complement
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs require de before their complement or a following infinitive. English often absorbs this de into the verb’s translation: dejar de means “to stop doing,” while disfrutar de means “to enjoy.”

example.en: I stopped smoking.

cards.noteEn: Que introduces a clause after verbs such as creer, saber, esperar, or decir. English often uses “that,” but may leave it unstated.

example.en: I think that Ana is coming.

cards.answerEn: myself; marks the speaker in a reflexive verb

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone opens up and shares personal feelings with another person?
cards.answerEn: Use the matching form of abrirse, followed by a and the person they open up to.
cards.noteEn: Abrirse literally suggests opening oneself, but with a person it means becoming emotionally honest or sharing private thoughts. The small pronoun changes with the person opening up: me abro, te abres, se abre, nos abrimos, and so on. The a before the listener stays.

example.es: Luis se abrió a su amiga.
example.en: Luis opened up to his friend.

cards.answerEn: I opened up; I would open up (a special past form)
cards.noteEn: Abriera is a past subjunctive form of abrir. The subjunctive is a special verb form used when an action is wanted, attempted, doubted, or otherwise not presented as a plain fact. With me and a person introduced by a, abrirse means to open up emotionally.

example.es: Ella quería que yo me abriera más.
example.en: She wanted me to open up more.

cards.answerEn: to; introduces the person someone opens up to
cards.noteEn: The expression abrirse a alguien uses a before the person who receives the honest or personal disclosure.

example.en: I opened up to a friend.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

example.en: We can enter now.

cards.noteEn: Herir can describe a physical wound or emotional hurt, especially with sentimientos (“feelings”).

example.en: I did not want to hurt her feelings.

cards.noteEn: Te can mean “to you” when you are the recipient or the person affected by an action. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.en: I’m sending you a message.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone likes doing an activity?
cards.answerEn: Use me, te, or le for the person, then gusta, then the action verb in its basic form.
cards.noteEn: Spanish builds this idea as the activity being pleasing to someone. The action verb stays in its dictionary form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir, and gusta remains singular for one whole activity.

example.en: I like reading.

cards.answerEn: you like; is pleasing to you

cards.questionEn: How do you say that an action hurts or harms someone or something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of hacer with daño. Introduce a named affected person or thing with a, or mark the affected person with a small pronoun such as me, te, or le.
cards.noteEn: Hacer daño works as a unit for causing physical or emotional harm. The affected person can appear after a, as in hace daño a Pablo, or in a small pronoun: me hizo daño (“it hurt me”) and hacerte daño (“to hurt you”). Hacer changes for person and time; daño stays unchanged.

example.es: Ese comentario le hizo daño a Pablo.
example.en: That comment hurt Pablo.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; introduces the person or group harmed
cards.noteEn: After hacer daño, a introduces the affected person, animal, group, or thing.

example.es: El ruido hace daño a los animales.
example.en: The noise harms animals.

cards.noteEn: Pues often connects a conclusion or next step to what was just said. In conversation, it can work like English 'so,' 'then,' or a second 'well.'

example.en: Then we will continue with the plan.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; introduces the person who likes something
cards.noteEn: With gustar, a can introduce or clarify the person experiencing the liking. A quien means “to whom” in the Spanish structure even when natural English simply says “who likes.”

example.es: Es una amiga a quien le gusta bailar.
example.en: She is a friend who likes dancing.

cards.answerEn: me (after a preposition such as para)
cards.noteEn: Spanish uses mí after most prepositions. The written accent distinguishes mí (“me”) from mi (“my”).

example.en: This gift is for me.

cards.answerEn: marks me as the person who likes something
cards.noteEn: With gustar, Spanish presents the liked thing as pleasing to a person. Me identifies the speaker as that person; it does not become a separate English word when the natural translation uses “I.”

example.en: I like coffee.

cards.answerEn: I like; is pleasing to me
cards.noteEn: With me before it, gusta expresses that one thing or situation is pleasing to the speaker. The liked thing controls the verb: use gusta for one thing and gustan for more than one.

example.en: I like this book.

cards.noteEn: Lo replaces a masculine singular thing, or sometimes a whole idea, as the direct object. It normally appears before a conjugated verb.

example.es: Tengo el libro y lo leo.
example.en: I have the book and I’m reading it.

cards.promptEs: lo, la, los, las delante de un verbo conjugado
cards.questionEn: Where do you put the Spanish word for “it” or “them” when the main verb already shows who acts and when?
cards.answerEn: Put lo, la, los, or las directly before that verb.
cards.noteEn: These short words replace the person or thing directly affected by the action; that role is called the direct object. Choose lo or los for a masculine thing, la or las for a feminine thing, and match singular or plural. Before a verb form such as conté or vimos, write the short word separately in front: lo conté, las vimos. With an unchanged dictionary form, it can instead attach to the end, as in verlo.

example.en: The movie—we watched it yesterday.

cards.noteEn: Mejor compares one option with another. It does not change for gender: una solución mejor and un plan mejor both use mejor.

example.en: We need a better idea.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone does something better than someone else?
cards.answerEn: Use mejor for “better,” then que before the person or thing being compared.
cards.noteEn: Mejor already contains the idea of “more good” or “better,” so do not add más before it. When mejor describes how an action is done, it does not change for gender or number. Que introduces the other side of the comparison.

example.en: Ana cooks better than I do.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of ir (“to go”), then a, then the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Ir changes to match the person: voy a means “I am going to,” vas a means “you are going to,” and va a means “he/she is going to.” The final action stays in its unchanged -ar, -er, or -ir form. This pattern expresses a plan, intention, or expected future event.
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is going to do something?

example.en: I am going to study.

cards.answerEn: to (part of ir a + infinitive, going to do something)
to hurt you; to cause you harm (with daño)
cards.noteEn: Hacerte joins the unchanged verb hacer to te, which identifies one familiar person as affected. In hacerte daño, daño supplies the harm and the complete expression means to hurt you.

example.en: I do not want to hurt you.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.

example.en: I want to help you.

cards.promptEs: más + nombre + del/de la/de los/de las que + verbo
cards.questionEn: How do you say “more of something than someone needs, uses, or can provide”?
cards.answerEn: Put más before the naming word, then use del que, de la que, de los que, or de las que before the second action. Match el, la, los, or las to that naming word.
cards.noteEn: A naming word is a noun such as tiempo, agua, libros, or horas. The article in the comparison repeats its gender and number: más tiempo del que, más agua de la que, más libros de los que, and más horas de las que. Del combines de and el. The following verb states the amount on the other side of the comparison.

example.es: Tenemos más tiempo del que necesitamos.
example.en: We have more time than we need.

cards.answerEn: than what; combines de + el in an amount comparison
cards.noteEn: Before que and a complete second action, del can refer back to a masculine singular amount or thing being compared. El matches that earlier noun, as in más tiempo del que necesitamos (“more time than we need”).

example.es: Compró más pan del que podía comer.
example.en: He bought more bread than he could eat.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes del que in an amount comparison
cards.noteEn: In más + noun + del que, que connects the amount named before del with the full action used as the other side of the comparison.

example.es: Hay más trabajo del que pensábamos.
example.en: There is more work than we thought.

cards.answerEn: you could; you would be able to
cards.noteEn: Podrías is the conditional, or “would,” form of poder for one familiar person. Poder changes to the irregular stem podr- and adds -ías; the following action stays in its unchanged dictionary form.

example.en: You could come tomorrow.

cards.answerEn: to hurt me; to do harm to me (with daño supplied by context)
cards.noteEn: Hacerme joins the unchanged verb hacer to me, which marks the speaker as affected. When daño has already been named, hacerme can carry the sense of doing that harm to me without repeating daño.

example.en: You could not hurt me that much.

cards.noteEn: Nunca usually means “never.” Inside a clause about what someone could possibly do, natural English can use “ever” because the negative or limiting force comes from the wider comparison.

example.es: Es más de lo que podría gastar nunca.
example.en: It is more than I could ever spend.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; introduces an emphasized object such as a mí
cards.noteEn: A stressed form such as a mí can repeat a short object pronoun such as me for contrast or emphasis. English normally expresses the emphasis through stress rather than an extra word.

example.en: You cannot see me in particular.

cards.noteEn: A speaker can use ¿sabes? to introduce a thought or draw the listener's attention, without literally testing what the listener knows.

example.en: You know? I think you're right.

cards.noteEn: Penetrado is penetrar's completed-action form. It can describe entering something physically or, figuratively, reaching beneath the surface of a person's thoughts or feelings.

example.es: La luz ha penetrado en la habitación.
example.en: The light has entered the room.

cards.answerEn: into; introduces what is entered after penetrar
cards.noteEn: Penetrar en presents a movement or reach into a place, material, subject, or person's inner world.

example.es: El agua penetró en la pared.
example.en: The water seeped into the wall.

cards.noteEn: As a noun, interior can mean the inside of something. Applied to a person, it can refer figuratively to private thoughts, feelings, or character.

example.es: Guardaba ese miedo en su interior.
example.en: She kept that fear inside herself.

cards.answerEn: of; among (introducing a type or group)
cards.noteEn: In de los de or de las de, this first de places someone among a recognizable type of people.

example.es: Pablo es de los de llegar pronto.
example.en: Pablo is one of those people who arrive early.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.answerEn: you will meet; you will get to know
cards.noteEn: Conocerás is the future form of conocer for one familiar person. With people not yet known, conocer often means to meet or become acquainted with them, not merely to know a fact.

example.en: You will meet my friends tomorrow.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.

example.en: Marta will call tomorrow.

cards.noteEn: The comic uses the formerly common accent in sólo. Current standard spelling normally writes solo without an accent when it means “only,” unless an accent is exceptionally needed to prevent genuine ambiguity.

example.en: I only need a minute.

cards.questionEn: Why can a Spanish sentence contain both no and another negative word?
cards.answerEn: When the second negative word follows the verb, keep no before the verb too.
cards.noteEn: Spanish commonly uses matching negative words together. No tiene ninguna means “it does not have any”; it does not become a positive meaning as two negatives sometimes do in formal English.

example.en: I do not have any doubt.

cards.noteEn: Verás keeps the whole verb ver and adds -ás, the future ending for one familiar person.

example.en: You will see the result tomorrow.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something will never happen again?
cards.noteEn: Nunca supplies ‘never’ and más extends it to ‘again’ or ‘anymore.’ If the phrase follows a verb that already has no before it, Spanish keeps both negatives.

example.en: I never want to see it again.

cards.noteEn: After nunca, más extends the negative into the future: nunca más means ‘never again.’

example.en: He never came back again.
